pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Erosion and weathering (measuring the effects)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Science working scientifically — take measurements, gather and record data to answer questions; Rocks):** Pupils make observations and measurements providing evidence of weathering and [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS2-1].

- **Standards — US (NGSS 4-ESS2-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS2-1].

- **Operational details:** This is a PROCEDURAL / investigation node — the goal is the SCIENTIFIC PROCESS of gathering evidence, not just the facts. First nail the distinction: weathering = rock broken down IN PLACE (frost cracking, plant roots, abrasion); erosion = the broken material MOVED away (by water, wind, ice). Then children run fair tests measuring an effect or a RATE — e.g. how much soil a stream washes away with vs without plant cover, or how wind speed changes sand movement — controlling variables and recording measurements. The heart is: change one agent/condition, measure the effect, compare. Stream-tables and shake-jar abrasion tests are the classic vehicles. Emphasise fair testing (same rock, same time, one variable changed) and quantifying (mass lost, distance moved, particles rounded).
bestPractices: Lock down weathering (break-down in place) vs erosion (transport away) before measuring — the investigation depends on the distinction.
Run FAIR TESTS: change one agent/condition (water flow, slope, plant cover, wind speed) and measure the effect while holding others constant.
Quantify effects — mass of material lost, distance sediment travels, how rounded particles become — so evidence is measured, not just described.
Use classic vehicles: a stream-table for water erosion, a shake-jar for abrasion/weathering, ice-in-cracks for freeze-thaw.
Connect measured results back to real landscapes (why a bare slope gullies, why a planted bank holds).
keyRepresentations: A stream-table (sloped tray of soil/sand with controllable water flow).
A shake-jar abrasion test (rock chips shaken, measuring rounding/sediment produced).
A fair-test comparison table (variable changed → measured effect).
Before/after landscape photos or profiles showing change.
commonMisconceptions: 'Weathering and erosion are the same' — conflating break-down with transport.
'Erosion is always fast/dramatic' — missing that much erosion is slow and gradual.
'Plants cause erosion' — not recognising vegetation usually PROTECTS soil (roots bind it), though roots can also weather rock.
'Harder rocks don't weather' — all rock weathers, just at different rates.
'A single trial proves it' — not valuing repeats/fair tests and measurement.
'Water only erodes, never deposits' — forgetting eroded material is dropped elsewhere.

learn.summary: Ages 9–10 Earth science: this is a PROCEDURAL investigation node whose goal is the scientific process of gathering measured evidence of weathering and erosion, not just the facts. Learners must first distinguish weathering (rock broken down into smaller pieces without being carried away — e.g. frost cracking, plant roots; abrasion, where pieces grind against each other, is often counted as weathering, although it happens while material is being moved) from erosion (the broken material moved away by water, ice, or wind), then run fair tests that change one agent/condition, measure an effect or rate, and compare. Classic vehicles are a stream-table for water erosion, a shake-jar abrasion test, and a freeze-thaw demonstration. Emphasise fair testing (same rock, same time, one variable changed) and quantifying (mass lost, distance moved, particles rounded), then connect measured results back to real landscapes.

activities.title: Stream-table fair test: does plant cover change how much soil erodes?
feedback: If a learner changes more than one thing at once (e.g. adds plants AND lowers the slope), point out the test is no longer fair: 'We can't tell which change caused the difference — hold everything else the same and change only the plant cover.'
If a learner trusts a single trial, prompt: 'Would you get the same grams if you ran it again? Repeat it and see whether the result holds.'

If a learner says plants cause erosion, show the two measured totals: the planted run usually loses less soil because roots bind it — though note roots can also help weather rock in place, which is a different process. How much less erodes depends on soil, slope and flow, so rely on the measured numbers rather than assuming a dramatic drop.
activities.rationale: A live, manipulable test-bench lets learners do the fair test and read out rate change with each variable, turning 'what speeds erosion' into measured evidence rather than a described fact. Sliders, a plant-cover toggle, a grams-lost meter, and a logged comparison table are optional concrete ways to scaffold the one-variable-at-a-time discipline.
sourceClaims: Weathering breaks rock down in place (freeze-thaw, biological, abrasion) while erosion transports the material; vegetation cover generally reduces soil erosion.
learnerActions: Build or use a sloped tray of soil/sand with a controllable water source (a real sand/soil stream-table, or a screen bench with sliders for slope and rainfall/flow and a plant-cover toggle).
Run a baseline trial: tilt the tray, set a steady water flow, run it, and measure the soil washed into the catch tray (grams lost) and how far the sediment travelled.
Change exactly ONE variable — add a mat of plant roots — keeping slope, flow, soil, and time identical, then rerun and measure again.
Record both trials in a comparison table (variable changed → measured effect) and state which single variable differed.
Repeat the trial at least once to check whether the result holds, then compare the plant-cover and bare totals.
activities.intendedInsight: Erosion is the transport of broken material, its rate can be measured and changed, and vegetation (root binding) generally reduces soil erosion rather than causing it — a conclusion backed by numbers from a controlled comparison.

activities.title: Shake-jar abrasion + freeze-thaw: separating break-down from transport
feedback: If a learner says 'the rock eroded' for breaking in place, separate the steps: 'Did the pieces move away, or just break? Breaking where it sits is weathering.'
If a learner treats moved material as having 'disappeared', ask 'where did the washed-off bits go?' and name the settling stage as deposition.

If a learner sees no obvious rounding and concludes nothing happened, point to the fines and clouded water — abrasion is real but slow, so the worn-off sediment is the measurable evidence; and remember sugar cubes only model rock and break, round and dissolve much faster.
activities.rationale: Classifying each observation as weathering or erosion directly targets the central conflation, and running abrasion and freeze-thaw as separate demonstrations lets learners attach 'broken in place' versus 'carried away' to the right evidence.
sourceClaims: Weathering breaks rock down in place (freeze-thaw, biological, abrasion) while erosion transports the material; vegetation cover generally reduces soil erosion.
learnerActions: Shake rock chips or gravel in a jar (with some water in it if you want to see clouding) and look for the signs of abrasion — fine sediment produced, water clouding if water is present, and edges gradually dulling. Visible rounding is slow, so the fine material worn off is the clearest short-term evidence that abrasion (weathering) is happening. Sugar cubes can stand in to show the idea quickly, but they dissolve in water and break far faster than rock, so use them only to illustrate the process, not to judge real rounding or rates.
Add water, swirl, then pour the water off into another container and watch where the broken bits settle — material carried away in the water and dropped elsewhere is erosion followed by deposition.

Run a freeze-thaw demonstration: soak a porous block or fill a crack in it with water (keep it wet between cycles), then repeatedly freeze and thaw it — as the water freezes it turns to ice and expands, pushing on the crack walls. Over many cycles this can widen the crack, flake off bits or eventually split the block, though a few classroom cycles may show only small changes; nothing is carried away (weathering in place).
For each observation, state out loud whether it shows weathering or erosion and what the evidence is.
Record how rounded/dulled the particles became and roughly how much sediment/fines were produced.
activities.intendedInsight: Weathering (broken where it sits) and erosion (carried away) are distinct processes; freeze-thaw and abrasion both weather rock, and once material moves it is eventually deposited somewhere else.

activities.title: Reading real landscapes: evidence of change over time
feedback: If a learner says 'nothing happened' to the year-apart bank, use the photos to measure the small change: slow change still counts as erosion.
If a learner thinks only sudden events count, contrast a flood with gradual year-on-year wearing — both are erosion at different rates.
If a learner thinks harder rocks don't weather, note that all rock weathers, just at different rates.
activities.rationale: Connecting measured investigation results back to real landscapes and reading before/after images addresses the 'erosion is always fast' and 'hard rock doesn't weather' misconceptions, and requires learners to produce evidence of change rather than only recall definitions.
learnerActions: Examine two photos of the same riverbank (or slope) taken about a year apart and describe what has changed.
Measure or estimate the small change (e.g. how far the bank edge retreated) and argue whether water could still be eroding it even though the change looks minor.
Classify features on a landscape image by the agent that shaped them (frost-cracked cliff, wind-carved rock, river-cut valley) and say whether each is mainly weathering or erosion.
Explain, using your measured stream-table results, why a bare slope often gullies and loses more soil while a planted bank usually holds better — and say whether your own numbers showed this.
activities.intendedInsight: Much erosion is slow and gradual, not only dramatic floods; measured change over time is still evidence, and features in real landscapes record the agents (water, ice, wind, vegetation) that acted on them.

constraints: Lock down the weathering (break-down in place) vs erosion (transport away) distinction before measuring — the whole investigation depends on it.
Fair tests require changing one agent/condition (water flow, slope, plant cover, wind speed) while holding everything else constant; otherwise the measured effect cannot be attributed to one cause.
Effects must be quantified — mass of material lost, distance sediment travels, degree of particle rounding/fines produced — so evidence is measured, not just described.

Classification/matching tasks (weathering vs erosion examples, agent ↔ effect, reading a results graph) and tap-to-reveal landscape labelling reinforce vocabulary and interpretation but do not themselves elicit the hands-on measurement and fair-testing that define this procedural node; use them as complements, not substitutes.

A virtual stream-table gives clean read-outs but is a model; a real sand/soil stream-table and shake-jar abrasion test are essential hands-on complements so learners handle genuine material with real grain, texture, and water/sediment behaviour that a model only approximates.
Sugar cubes and other models stand in for rock to show the process faster but dissolve and break unrealistically; do not treat their rates or rounding as real rock behaviour.
A 3D terrain that erodes under rain is a richer, heavier alternative that adds spatial realism but is not required; the core target is controlled measurement and the weathering/erosion distinction.
Include deposition explicitly: eroded material does not disappear, it settles elsewhere.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources are marked verified:false and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims support the standard and the weathering/erosion/vegetation principles but do not establish the comparative or empirical effectiveness of any specific activity or medium.

The legacy row at times implied a live bench is uniquely able to teach this ('a static resource can't', dialogue 'can't run the tests'); these have been softened to scoped affordances/limits. Static and recognition resources can still support classification and interpretation.

The original 'plants cause erosion' misconception handling is retained but nuanced: vegetation generally protects soil by binding it, while roots can also contribute to weathering rock — keep these two effects distinct for learners.
Deposition is central to the assessment but was only a secondary evidence point in the original learn section; it has been promoted into the activities.

The original recommendation's 'eroded total plummets' was softened to a measured, conditions-dependent reduction; the freeze-thaw mechanism was clarified (water freezes to ice and expands over repeated freeze–thaw cycles).

The shake-jar rounding observation was made realistic: visible rounding of real rock is slow over a short lesson, so the measurable short-term evidence is the fines/sediment produced; conclusions about 'rounding' remain approximate.

probeDeeper: In the jar, did the cubes get moved or just broken? Which of those is weathering?
Where did the broken pieces go once the water carried them? What do we call that?
The riverbank changed only a little in a year. Could water still be eroding it? How?
Which agent — water, ice, wind, or plant roots — could break a rock without moving it at all?
assess.correctAnswer: The child shakes the cubes and shows they break down and round in place (weathering), then shows the broken bits carried away by the water and settling elsewhere (erosion = movement, then deposition), and reads the riverbank photos as material worn away and moved over the year — keeping 'breaking in place' separate from 'being moved'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Weathering and erosion are the same thing — uses them interchangeably ('the rock eroded away' for breaking in place)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront it — weathering breaks the rock where it sits, erosion carries the pieces away; demonstrate each step on its own.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels breaking-in-place as erosion, or transport as weathering; can't separate the two observations.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores deposition — the moved material just 'disappears' rather than settling somewhere else
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold — 'where did the washed-off bits go?' and introduce deposition as the settling stage.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes erosion but never says where the sediment ends up.

errorPatterns.pattern: Erosion is always fast and dramatic (a flood) — slow change doesn't count ('nothing happened' to the year-apart bank)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast rapid vs slow rates; use the photos to measure the small change over a year.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Only accepts sudden events as erosion; dismisses the small year-on-year change in the photos.

responseLevels.gap: Uses weathering and erosion interchangeably; can't produce evidence of either.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes weathering (broken in place) from erosion (moved) with matched evidence, names several agents, and accounts for deposition and slow rates — reading the photos as evidence of change over time.
responseLevels.partial: Produces the observations and names the agents but blurs weathering vs erosion, or ignores where the moved material goes.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two photos of the same riverbank a year apart, and a jar where you can shake sugar cubes ('rocks') in water. Show me how you'd get evidence of weathering and of erosion, and as you go, tell me which is which and what your evidence shows.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The weathering/erosion conflation is the crux: many children use the two words as synonyms. Watching whether they attach 'broken where it sits' vs 'carried away' to the right observation separates naming the agents from understanding the two distinct processes — and whether they notice deposition, which is routinely ignored.
